How do C++ templates actually work during the compilation process?

C++ templates are not compiled immediately when defined. Instead, they act like blueprints. The actual compilation happens during instantiation — when you use the template with a specific type, like `std::vector<int>`. At that point, the compiler generates a concrete version of the function or class by substituting the template parameter (e.g., `T`) with the actual type (`int`). This process is called template instantiation. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/templates)

The cutter doesn't bake the cookie — it only shapes it when applied. Similarly, the template doesn't generate code until it's used with a specific type. The compiler then ""stamps out"" a version of the function or class tailored to that type. This is why templates are resolved at compile time, not run time. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/function_template)

What exactly is object slicing in C++ and how does passing by reference prevent it?

Object slicing happens when a derived class object is assigned to or passed as a base class object by value. Because the destination is only large enough for the base class, the derived part (member variables and functions specific to the derived class) gets ""sliced off."" Passing by reference (or pointer) avoids this because no copying occurs. Instead, the function receives a reference to the original object, preserving its actual type. What are the theoretical performance tradeoffs between a linked list and a dynamic array?

Great question! Let's integrate what we've learned about memory layout and access patterns. A dynamic array (like `std::vector`) stores elements contiguously, which gives excellent cache locality and fast random access—O(1) time. However, inserting or deleting in the middle requires shifting all subsequent elements, which is O(n).

In contrast, a linked list allocates nodes non-contiguously, with each node pointing to the next. This means no shifting is needed during insertions or deletions—once you find the location, the operation itself is O(1). But finding that location requires traversal from the head, so random access is O(n), and cache performance is poorer due to non-local memory access.

So yes, if you're doing many middle insertions/deletions, a linked list can be more efficient for those specific operations. But if you're mostly accessing elements by index or appending to the end, a dynamic array is typically faster in practice due to memory efficiency. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector)
